## Before we get started

In [part I](w11b_nfcore1.qmd), we introduced nf-core pipelines
and did a test run of the nf-core _rnaseq_ pipeline.
On this page, we will run that pipeline on the @garrigós2025 RNA-seq data.

### Learning goals

Specifically, you will learn:

- How to prepare the inputs for an nf-core pipeline run,
  including a sample sheet and reference genome files
- How these pipelines can be run with a single command,
  while they submit jobs to the Slurm scheduler at OSC
- How to monitor pipeline progress
- How to find and interpret the output files produced by the pipeline

### Getting ready

1. At <https://ondemand.osc.edu>,
   start a VS Code session in `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER`.

2. In your VS Code terminal, go to your working dir for this week:

   ```bash
   cd week11
   ```

## Preparation for the run

For the pipeline run with the @garrigós2025 data, we need to start with some prep:

1. Download the **reference genome assembly**.
2. Create a "**sample sheet**" to tell the pipeline about our input FASTQ files.
3. Create a small "**config file**" so Nextflow knows how to submit Slurm batch
   jobs at OSC.

First, we need to get set up. Make sure you are in your `week11` dir
(if you're still in the `testrun` dir from part I, move up with `cd ..`),
and then:

Create a README file and open it:

```bash
touch README.md
```

Paste the following into it (with your own name and username),
and then run the `mkdir` command to create dirs for scripts and metadata:

````{.markdown .file filename="README.md (excerpt)"}
## Running the nf-core rnaseq pipeline on the Garrigos data

- Create dirs for scripts and metadata:
````

### Download the reference genome assembly

The `garrigos` repo contains the reference genome annotation (GTF) file,
but not the assembly (FASTA) file, which was too large to include.
Download the assembly from NCBI with the `wget` command,
like you did in [Lecture A](w11a_data.qmd#wget)
(this time into `garrigos/ref`):

````{.markdown .file filename="README.md (excerpt)"}
- Download the reference genome assembly:

```bash
URL=https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genomes/all/GCF/016/801/865/GCF_016801865.2_TS_CPP_V2/GCF_016801865.2_TS_CPP_V2_genomic.fna.gz
wget -P ../garrigos/ref "$URL"
```
````

### Create a sample sheet

This pipeline requires a "sample sheet" as one of its inputs.
In the sample sheet, you should provide the paths to your FASTQ files
and specify the so-called strandedness of your RNA-seq library.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### RNA-seq library strandedness _(Click to expand)_
During RNA-seq library prep, information about the directionality of the original
RNA transcripts can be retained (resulting in a "stranded" library) or lost
(resulting in an "unstranded" library: specify `unstranded` in the sample sheet).

In turn, stranded libraries can be prepared either in
reverse-stranded (`reverse`, by far the most common) or
forward-stranded (`forward`) fashion.
For more information about library strandedness,
see [this page](https://www.azenta.com/blog/stranded-versus-non-stranded-rna-seq).

The pipeline also allows for a fourth option: `auto`,
in which case the strandedness is automatically determined at the start of the pipeline
by pseudo-mapping a small proportion of the data with Salmon.
:::

The sample sheet should be a plain-text comma-separated values (CSV) file.
Here is the example file from the
[pipeline's documentation](https://nf-co.re/rnaseq/3.26.0/docs/usage#samplesheet-input):

```{.file filename="samplesheet.csv (example from the pipeline docs)"}
sample,fastq_1,fastq_2,strandedness
CONTROL_REP1,AEG588A1_S1_L002_R1_001.fastq.gz,AEG588A1_S1_L002_R2_001.fastq.gz,auto
CONTROL_REP1,AEG588A1_S1_L003_R1_001.fastq.gz,AEG588A1_S1_L003_R2_001.fastq.gz,auto
CONTROL_REP1,AEG588A1_S1_L004_R1_001.fastq.gz,AEG588A1_S1_L004_R2_001.fastq.gz,auto
```

So, we need a header row with column names, and then one row per pair of FASTQ files^[
In the example above, sample `CONTROL_REP1` was sequenced on three lanes,
so it has three rows, which the pipeline will merge.
We have one pair of FASTQ files per sample, so we'll have one row per sample.].
The file should have the following columns:

- `sample`: Sample ID (we will simply use the part of the file name shared by R1 and R2)
- `fastq_1`: R1 FASTQ file path (including the dir, unless these files are in your working dir)
- `fastq_2`: R2 FASTQ file path (idem)
- `strandedness`: The library's strandedness,
  `unstranded`, `reverse`, `forward`, or `auto`.
  This data is forward-stranded, so we'll use `forward`^[
  If you have your own RNA-seq data, whoever did the library prep should know
  what the strandedness is.
  If you really don't know, use `auto` to let the pipeline figure it out.].

You could create this file manually in a text editor,
but that would be tedious and error-prone with many samples.
Instead, we will create it with a `for` loop that is very similar
to the loops we used last week to submit a batch job for each sample:

````{.markdown .file filename="README.md (excerpt)"}
- Create a samplesheet:

```bash
# Create the file with a header line
echo "sample,fastq_1,fastq_2,strandedness" > metadata/nfc-samplesheet.csv

# Add a row for each sample
for fastq_r1 in ../garrigos/fastq/*_R1.fastq.gz; do
    fastq_r2=${fastq_r1/_R1/_R2}
    sample_id=$(basename "$fastq_r1" _R1.fastq.gz)
    echo "$sample_id,$fastq_r1,$fastq_r2,forward" >> metadata/nfc-samplesheet.csv
done
```
````

- The first `echo` command creates the sample sheet file with the header line.
- In the loop, we only loop over the R1 FASTQ files,
  and infer the name of the corresponding R2 file by replacing `_R1` with `_R2`
  with parameter expansion: the `${var/find/replace}` syntax
  (see [week 7](../week07/w7b_scripts2.qmd#parameter-expansion)).
- `basename` removes both the dir name and the `_R1.fastq.gz` suffix
  from the R1 file path, leaving the sample ID (e.g., `S63`).
  We store its output in a variable with command substitution, `$()`
  (both are covered on the optional
  [shell scripting self-study page](../bonus/shell-scripting.qmd#commands-to-extract-parts-of-paths)).
- We _append_ (`>>`) each row to the sample sheet
  so that we keep the header line and the rows for previous samples.

<details class="details-quiz">
<summary>What would go wrong if the loop went over all FASTQ files (`../garrigos/fastq/*.fastq.gz`) instead of only the R1 files?</summary>

_The answer will be added after class._

The sample sheet would have two rows per sample.
The rows for the R1 files would be fine, but each R2 file would also get its own row:

- Because the R2 file name doesn't contain `_R1`, the R2 file would be used as both `fastq_1` and `fastq_2`.
- `basename` wouldn't remove the `_R1.fastq.gz` suffix, so the sample ID would be e.g. `S63_R2.fastq.gz`.

Depending on the pipeline's sample sheet checks, it would either stop with an error,
or (worse) process these rows as extra, bogus samples.

</details>

Run the code above and check the contents of your newly created sample sheet file:

```bash
# [Run this directly in the terminal]
head -n 5 metadata/nfc-samplesheet.csv
```
```bash-out
sample,fastq_1,fastq_2,strandedness
S63,../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz,../garrigos/fastq/S63_R2.fastq.gz,forward
S64,../garrigos/fastq/S64_R1.fastq.gz,../garrigos/fastq/S64_R2.fastq.gz,forward
S65,../garrigos/fastq/S65_R1.fastq.gz,../garrigos/fastq/S65_R2.fastq.gz,forward
S66,../garrigos/fastq/S66_R1.fastq.gz,../garrigos/fastq/S66_R2.fastq.gz,forward
```

### Create a configuration file

One of the strengths of Nextflow/nf-core pipelines is that they can be run
on a wide variety of compute infrastructures,
from a laptop to HPC clusters and cloud computing.
Our [test run](w11b_nfcore1.qmd#test-run-the-rnaseq-pipeline) used the simplest scenario,
running everything "locally" on a single node.
However, for our real data run,
we want to have the pipeline submit Slurm batch jobs so it will efficiently
run in parallel across multiple nodes.

To tell the pipeline to submit Slurm batch jobs for us,
we will again use a `nextflow.config` file,
like the one you [created for the test run](w11b_nfcore1.qmd#create-a-configuration-file).
Because Nextflow only automatically reads a `nextflow.config` file in the dir from which you run it,
the file in your `testrun` dir won't be used,
and we need to create a new one in your `week11` dir.

- Create the config file:

  ```bash
  touch nextflow.config
  ```

- Since the pipeline has many good default settings for batch jobs,
  we can keep this config file very simple.
  Besides the container dir setting from the test run,
  we only need to specify our "executor" program (Slurm)
  and the OSC project to be used for Slurm job submissions.
  Open the newly created `nextflow.config` file in the VS Code editor
  and paste the following into it:

  ```{.groovy .file filename="nextflow.config"}
  apptainer.cacheDir='/fs/ess/PAS3493/share/nxf-containers'
  process.executor='slurm'
  process.clusterOptions='--account=PAS3493'
  ```

  The two new settings are in the `process` scope,
  which contains settings for the jobs that Nextflow runs for each step of the pipeline.

## Write a shell script to run the pipeline

As mentioned [in part I](w11b_nfcore1.qmd#overview-of-running-an-nf-core-pipeline),
for this larger pipeline run,
we will also submit the `nextflow run` command _itself_ as a Slurm batch job
via a shell script.
So, there are two "layers" of batch jobs:
the main Nextflow process, for which we submit a batch job ourselves,
and the jobs that this process submits for each step and sample:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A["You:<br>sbatch scripts/nfc-rnaseq.sh"] --> B["Main Nextflow job<br>(1 core, runs for the whole pipeline)"]
  B -->|sbatch| C["TrimGalore job (S63)"]
  B -->|sbatch| D["STAR job (S63)"]
  B -->|sbatch| E["... (hundreds more)"]
```

Let's go through the key parts of this shell script.

### Processing arguments passed to the script

As we've often done with shell scripts to run bioinformatics tools,
we'll keep the shell script flexible by having it accept arguments that represent
the inputs and outputs of the pipeline:

- Input 1: The sample sheet
- Input 2: The FASTA reference genome assembly file
- Input 3: The GTF reference genome annotation file
- Output 1: The desired output dir for the final pipeline output
- Output 2: The desired Nextflow "work dir" for all job outputs, including intermediate files

```{.bash .file filename="scripts/nfc-rnaseq.sh (excerpt)"}
# Copy the placeholder variables
samplesheet=$1
fasta=$2
gtf=$3
outdir=$4
workdir=$5
```

When building the command below,
we'll use these variables to refer to the input/output paths.

### Writing the `nextflow run` command

Here is the part of the command that includes **general Nextflow options**:

```{.bash .file filename="scripts/nfc-rnaseq.sh (excerpt)"}
nextflow run nf-core/rnaseq \
    -r 3.26.0 \
    -profile apptainer \
    -resume \
    -work-dir "$workdir" \
    -ansi-log false \
```

- Like in the [test run](w11b_nfcore1.qmd#test-run-the-rnaseq-pipeline),
  our command starts with `nextflow run` followed by the pipeline name and version.
- The `-profile` will now simply be `apptainer` (i.e. omitting `test`).
- It's a good idea to always include the `-resume` option:
  it doesn't do anything when we run the pipeline for the first time^[
  Nextflow will even give a warning along these lines, but this is not a problem.],
  but if the run fails or we change a setting,
  we can simply resubmit the same script and the pipeline will pick up where it left off.
- We set the `-work-dir` to a dir within our project's Scratch dir (`/fs/scratch`),
  which is well suited for the many large intermediate files in the work dir
  due to its fast I/O and ample storage space.
  Recall that files in Scratch are automatically deleted after 60 days unused.
  That's fine for the work dir, which you only need until you're done with the run
  (e.g., to `-resume` it after a failure or after changing a setting).
  (Our final output dir, on the other hand, will be in our Project dir in `/fs/ess`.)
- The `-ansi-log false` option changes the logging format from what we
  saw in the test run to a more basic format that works much better with Slurm log files^[
  In this format, there is a separate line for each job rather than grouping jobs
  by process.].

Next, we'll add the **pipeline-specific options**,
starting with several _required_ options
(see the [pipeline's documentation](https://nf-co.re/rnaseq/3.26.0/docs/usage)),
which represent the inputs and outputs discussed above --- the paths to:

- **`--input`**: the "sample sheet"
- **`--fasta`**: the reference genome assembly FASTA file
- **`--gtf`**: the reference genome annotation GTF file
- **`--outdir`**: the output dir

This pipeline has different options for e.g. alignment and quantification.
We will stick close to the defaults,
which include read alignment with `STAR` and gene-level quantification with `Salmon`,
with two exceptions.
First, we want to remove reads that originate from ribosomal RNA
(this removal step is skipped by default).
Second, we need to change one setting to make the pipeline work with our GTF file
(more about this below).

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise: Find the right pipeline option
Take a look at the
["Parameters" tab on the pipeline's documentation website](https://nf-co.re/rnaseq/3.26.0/parameters):

1. Browse through the options for a bit to get a feel for the extent to which you
   can customize the pipeline.

2. Find the option to remove reads that originate from ribosomal RNA (rRNA).

<!----
<details><summary> _Click for the solution_ </summary>

The option to remove rRNA is **`--remove_ribo_rna`**.

</details>
---->
:::

As for the GTF setting:
one of the pipeline's QC steps summarizes from which types of genes ("biotypes")
the reads originate, such as protein-coding genes, long non-coding RNAs, and rRNA genes.
By default, the pipeline looks for this information in a `gene_biotype` field
on the exon lines of the GTF file.
But our GTF file, which comes from NCBI, only has that field on its gene lines,
and calls it `transcript_biotype` on its exon lines ---
so with the default setting, the pipeline would stop with an error.
To make it use the `transcript_biotype` field instead,
we will add **`--featurecounts_group_type transcript_biotype`**.

<details class="details-quiz">
<summary>What do you think would happen if you made a typo in a pipeline-specific option, e.g. `--remove_ribo_rnaa`?</summary>

_The answer will be added after class._

<!--
The pipeline would run anyway, but without removing rRNA!
nf-core pipelines only print a warning about unrecognized parameters
near the top of the log, and then ignore them.
(A typo in a general Nextflow option, like `-resum`, is different:
Nextflow will refuse to start and report an unknown option.)
So, always check the warnings and the parameter summary at the top of the log.
-->
</details>

### The final script

Now, we're ready to create the full shell script.

```bash
touch scripts/nfc-rnaseq.sh
# Then open the newly created script in the VS Code editor
```

Paste the following code into the script ---
this contains the discussed command and variables, as well as:

- The "standard shell" script header lines we've been using
- `#SBATCH` options for the main Nextflow process.
  We ask for 12 hours mostly because the resource requests for the jobs that
  Nextflow submits are rather large by default,
  such that these jobs may be queued for substantial amounts of time
  (without queueing time, the pipeline would finish in well under an hour).
  We also ask for 8 GB of memory, since the default 4 GB is not always enough
  for the main Nextflow process.
- Some `echo` reporting of arguments/variables, printing the date, etc.

```{.bash .file filename="scripts/nfc-rnaseq.sh"}
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --account=PAS3493
#SBATCH --time=12:00:00
#SBATCH --mem=8G
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL
#SBATCH --output=slurm-nfc-rnaseq-%j.out
set -euo pipefail

# Run the nf-core/rnaseq pipeline
# Usage: sbatch scripts/nfc-rnaseq.sh <sample sheet> <FASTA> <GTF> <output dir> <work dir>

# Load the Nextflow module
module load nextflow/25.04.6

# Copy the placeholder variables
samplesheet=$1
fasta=$2
gtf=$3
outdir=$4
workdir=$5

# Initial logging
echo "Starting script nfc-rnaseq.sh"
date
echo "Samplesheet:          $samplesheet"
echo "Reference FASTA:      $fasta"
echo "Reference GTF:        $gtf"
echo "Output dir:           $outdir"
echo "Nextflow work dir:    $workdir"
echo

# Create the output dirs
mkdir -p "$outdir" "$workdir"

# Run the workflow
nextflow run nf-core/rnaseq \
    -r 3.26.0 \
    -profile apptainer \
    -resume \
    -work-dir "$workdir" \
    -ansi-log false \
    --input "$samplesheet" \
    --fasta "$fasta" \
    --gtf "$gtf" \
    --outdir "$outdir" \
    --remove_ribo_rna \
    --featurecounts_group_type transcript_biotype

# Final logging
echo
echo "Successfully finished script nfc-rnaseq.sh"
date
```

<details class="details-quiz">
<summary>The pipeline runs tools like STAR that need many cores and lots of memory. So why is it fine that this script only asks for 1 core and 8 GB?</summary>

_The answer will be added after class._

<!--
The `#SBATCH` options are only for the "main" Nextflow process,
which merely orchestrates the pipeline and submits jobs.
The jobs that Nextflow submits for each step have their own resource requests,
which the pipeline sets for each step
(you could change these in your `nextflow.config` file, but we won't do that here).
-->
</details>

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
#### Setting the container dir in your own pipeline runs _(Click to expand)_

When you run Nextflow pipelines for your own research,
it's a good idea to also use a single dir for all Apptainer containers,
because they take up several GBs and can be reused across runs and pipelines.
Set `apptainer.cacheDir` in your `nextflow.config` file to a dir in your own project, e.g.:

```{.groovy .file filename="nextflow.config (excerpt)"}
apptainer.cacheDir='/fs/ess/<your-project>/containers'
```
:::

## Run the pipeline

Now that the shell script is ready,
you can run the pipeline on the @garrigós2025 data!
You will add the code to do so to the `README.md` file we created above.

### Define variables to pass to the shell script

First, define variables with the arguments needed to run the script:

````{.markdown .file filename="README.md (excerpt)"}
- Define the pipeline inputs and outputs:

```bash
# Inputs
samplesheet=metadata/nfc-samplesheet.csv
fasta=../garrigos/ref/GCF_016801865.2_TS_CPP_V2_genomic.fna.gz
gtf=../garrigos/ref/annot.gtf.gz

# Outputs
outdir=results/nfc-rnaseq
workdir=/fs/scratch/PAS3493/$USER/week11/nfc-rnaseq-work
```
````
Run the above lines in your terminal,
then check that the input files are present at the specified paths:

```bash
ls -lh "$samplesheet" "$fasta" "$gtf"
```
```bash-out
-rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 5.1M Sep 14 14:41 ../garrigos/ref/annot.gtf.gz
-rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 165M Dec 22  2022 ../garrigos/ref/GCF_016801865.2_TS_CPP_V2_genomic.fna.gz
-rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 2.5K Nov  2 14:39 metadata/nfc-samplesheet.csv
```

### Submit your shell script

Finally, add the code to submit the shell script into the `README.md` file,
and run it:

````{.markdown .file filename="README.md (excerpt)"}
- Submit the script to run the pipeline as a batch job:

```bash
sbatch scripts/nfc-rnaseq.sh "$samplesheet" "$fasta" "$gtf" "$outdir" "$workdir"
```
````

```bash-out-solo
Submitted batch job 42175708
```

<summary>Say you had changed all paths to absolute paths, and submitted this same `sbatch` command from a different dir. What do you think would happen?</summary>

_The answer will be added after class._

<!--
Nextflow only automatically reads a `nextflow.config` file in the dir from which you run it,
so it wouldn't find our config file and wouldn't know that it should submit Slurm jobs.
Instead, it would run all jobs "locally", inside the main Nextflow job.
That job only has 1 core, while steps like STAR request many more,
so the pipeline would quickly fail with an error like
`Process requirement exceeds available CPUs`.
-->
</details>

````{.markdown .file filename="README.md (full)"}
# RNA-seq analysis of _Culex pipiens_ with the nf-core rnaseq pipeline

- Author: Jane Doe
- Date: 2026-11-02
- This was run at the Ohio Supercomputer Center (OSC),
  in the dir `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/jdoe/week11`

## Running the nf-core rnaseq pipeline on the Garrigos data

- Create dirs for scripts and metadata:

```bash
mkdir scripts metadata
```

- Download the reference genome assembly:

```bash
URL=https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genomes/all/GCF/016/801/865/GCF_016801865.2_TS_CPP_V2/GCF_016801865.2_TS_CPP_V2_genomic.fna.gz
wget -P ../garrigos/ref "$URL"
```

- Create a samplesheet:

```bash
# Create the file with a header line
echo "sample,fastq_1,fastq_2,strandedness" > metadata/nfc-samplesheet.csv

# Add a row for each sample
for fastq_r1 in ../garrigos/fastq/*_R1.fastq.gz; do
    fastq_r2=${fastq_r1/_R1/_R2}
    sample_id=$(basename "$fastq_r1" _R1.fastq.gz)
    echo "$sample_id,$fastq_r1,$fastq_r2,forward" >> metadata/nfc-samplesheet.csv
done
```

- Define the pipeline inputs and outputs:

```bash
# Inputs
samplesheet=metadata/nfc-samplesheet.csv
fasta=../garrigos/ref/GCF_016801865.2_TS_CPP_V2_genomic.fna.gz
gtf=../garrigos/ref/annot.gtf.gz

# Outputs
outdir=results/nfc-rnaseq
workdir=/fs/scratch/PAS3493/$USER/week11/nfc-rnaseq-work
```

- Submit the script to run the pipeline as a batch job:

```bash
sbatch scripts/nfc-rnaseq.sh "$samplesheet" "$fasta" "$gtf" "$outdir" "$workdir"
```
````
</details>

Let's check whether your job has started running,
and if so, whether Nextflow has already spawned jobs:

```bash
# [Run this directly in the terminal]
squeue -u $USER -l
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
#### How to see the full names of jobs with long names _(Click to expand)_

Unfortunately, the columns in the output above are quite narrow,
so it's **not possible to see which step of the pipeline is being run by that job**.
The following (awful-looking!) code can be used to make that column much wider,
so you can see the jobs' full names, which makes clear which steps are being run:

```bash
# (The '%.100j' makes the NAME column 100 characters wide)
squeue -u $USER --format="%.9i %.9P %.100j %.8T %.10M %.10l %.4C %R %.16V"
```

See the [self-study page on Slurm](../bonus/slurm.qmd#monitoring-your-jobs-with-squeue)
for an explanation of this command,
and for how to make an alias for it so you don't have to type it out.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### You should also see the following warning among the job submissions _(Click to expand)_

This warning appears to be related to a small bug in the pipeline code that
should not affect the results:

```bash-out-solo
WARN: The operator `first` is useless when applied to a value channel which returns a single value by definition
```
:::

If any errors occur, they are reported in this file.
When a job fails because it ran out of memory or time,
the pipeline will by default retry it once, with increased resource requests.
Other errors, e.g. due to a problem with your input files,
will make the pipeline stop, and you will have to investigate the problem.

Your pipeline run may finish in as little as 15--30 minutes with our small dataset,
but this can vary substantially due to variation in Slurm queue times.
When the pipeline has finished,
make sure to pay attention to the message that is printed at the end of the log file ---
in the example below, the pipeline finished successfully:

```bash-out-solo
[ca/b7b202] Submitted process > NFCORE_RNASEQ:RNASEQ:BEDGRAPH_BEDCLIP_BEDGRAPHTOBIGWIG_REVERSE:UCSC_BEDGRAPHTOBIGWIG (S79)
[86/67dd0a] Submitted process > NFCORE_RNASEQ:RNASEQ:BEDGRAPH_BEDCLIP_BEDGRAPHTOBIGWIG_FORWARD:UCSC_BEDGRAPHTOBIGWIG (S64)
-[nf-core/rnaseq] Pipeline completed successfully -

Successfully finished script nfc-rnaseq.sh
Mon Nov 02 02:57:49 PM EST 2026
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### If your pipeline run fails _(Click to expand)_

When a job fails and the pipeline stops,
the end of the Slurm log file will show an error message like this one:

```bash-out-solo
ERROR ~ Error executing process > 'NFCORE_RNASEQ:RNASEQ:ALIGN_STAR:STAR_ALIGN (S63)'

Caused by:
  Process `NFCORE_RNASEQ:RNASEQ:ALIGN_STAR:STAR_ALIGN (S63)` terminated with an error exit status (1)

Command executed:
  # [...]

Command exit status:
  1

Command error:
  # [...the last lines of the job's standard error...]

Work dir:
  /fs/scratch/PAS3493/jelmer/week11/nfc-rnaseq-work/3f/a71c2e[...]
```

To troubleshoot:

1. Read the `Command error` section,
   which shows the last lines of what the failed job printed to standard error.
2. If that isn't enough, go to the job's `Work dir`,
   and check the `.command.err` and `.command.log` files there
   (and `.command.sh`, to see the exact command that was run).
3. Some errors occur before any job is run, e.g. a typo in an option or a missing input file.
   Those are shown in the Slurm log file too,
   with more details in the hidden file `.nextflow.log` in the dir from which you ran the pipeline.

After fixing the problem, submit the script again with the exact same `sbatch` command:
because the script uses `-resume`, the pipeline will pick up where it left off.
:::

### Overview

Once the pipeline run has finished,
take a look at the files and dirs in the specified output dir
(if your run hasn't finished yet,
look at the outputs of my run in `/fs/ess/PAS3493/share/week11/nfc-rnaseq` instead):

```bash
ls -lh results/nfc-rnaseq
```
<pre class="bash-out"><code>total 19K
drwxrwx---+  4 jelmer PAS0471 4.0K Nov  2 14:47 <span class="ls-blue">fastqc</span>

This looks much like the output of the
[test run in part I](w11b_nfcore1.qmd#main-output-files),
except that there is now a `sortmerna` dir because we removed rRNA,
and that there are no `bbsplit` and `salmon` dirs,
since those steps were only part of the test run.

Like in the test run, the two most important outputs are:

- The **MultiQC report** (`multiqc/star_salmon/multiqc_report.html`),
  which we'll take a closer look at below.
- The **gene count table** (`star_salmon/salmon.merged.gene_counts_length_scaled.tsv`),
  which you'll use for differential expression analysis in week 15!

### The MultiQC report

Open the MultiQC report like we've done with other HTML files:
download the file
(find it in the VS Code file browser on the left,
right-click on it, and select `Download...`) and then open it on your own computer
(alternatively, open the
**[copy of the MultiQC report on this website](../assets/multiqc_report_nfcore.html)**).
There's a lot of information in the report, so we'll just highlight a few things here.

<!-- TODO: re-check these notes and the screenshot with 3.26.0 (FastQC raw/trim/filt columns, %rRNA fix, paired-end row grouping) -->

The **General Statistics** table (the first section) is useful but also a bit tricky ---
some notes:

- Most of the table's content is also present in later graphs,
  but the table allows for comparisons across metrics.
- The `%rRNA` (% of reads identified as rRNA and removed by SortMeRNA)
  can only be found in this table.
- Many columns are shown and it can be useful to click **"Configure Columns"**
  and subset the table to only the columns you care about.
  In particular, it's best to _hide the columns with statistics from Samtools_,
  which can be confusing if not downright misleading
  (e.g., they count alignments rather than reads,
  so reads that map to multiple places are counted several times):
  in the "Configure Columns" dialog box,
  uncheck all boxes for stats with Samtools in their name.
- Unfortunately, there are multiple rows per sample
  (4 when the default columns are shown), in part because some stats are
  for R1 and R2 files separately, while others are for each sample as a whole.

![](/img/multiqc-nfc-rnaseq-table.png){fig-align="center" width="90%" .no-border fig-alt="The General Statistics table after selecting only a subset of columns."}

::: legend2
The General Statistics table after selecting only a subset of columns
:::

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

The **Qualimap** > **Genomic origin of reads** plot shows, for each sample,
the proportion of reads mapping to exonic vs. intronic vs. intergenic regions.
This is an important QC plot: the vast majority of your reads should be exonic^[
A lot of intronic content may indicate that you have a lot of pre-mRNA in your data;
this is more common when your library prep used rRNA depletion instead of poly-A selection.
A lot of intergenic content may indicate DNA contamination.
Poor genome annotation quality may also contribute to a low percentage of exonic reads.
The _RSeQC_ > _Read Distribution_ plot will show this with even more categories,
e.g. separately showing UTRs.].

![](/img/multiqc_genomic-origin.png){fig-align="center" width="90%" .no-border fig-alt="MultiQC stacked bar chart of Qualimap genomic origin for 20 samples. In every sample, roughly 85-87% of reads are exonic, with the remainder split between intronic and intergenic."}

::: legend2
This is a good result, with 80-90% of mapped reads in exonic regions.
:::

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

The **STAR** > **Alignment Scores** plot shows, for each sample,
the percentage of reads that were mapped.
Note that "Mapped to multiple loci" reads _are_ also included in the final counts,
and that "Unmapped: too short" really means unmapped rather than that the reads
were too short^[It says "too short" because the aligned part of the read was too short.].

![](/img/multiqc_star.png){fig-align="center" width="90%" .no-border fig-alt="MultiQC stacked bar chart of STAR alignment scores for 20 samples. In every sample, about 80-86% of reads are uniquely mapped, a few percent map to multiple loci, and the remaining 11-17% are unmapped because they are too short."}

::: legend2
This is a pretty good result, with 80-90% of reads mapped.
:::

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

The **RSeQC** > **Infer experiment** plot shows the library strandedness.
If your library is:

- Unstranded, there should be similar percentages of Sense and Antisense reads.
- Forward-stranded, the vast majority of reads should be Sense.
- Reverse-stranded, the vast majority of reads should be Antisense.

![](/img/multiqc_strandedness.png){fig-align="center" width="85%" .no-border fig-alt="MultiQC stacked bar chart of RSeQC inferred strandedness for 20 samples. In every sample, over 90% of reads are sense, with small fractions antisense and undetermined."}

::: legend2
This library is clearly forward-stranded, as we indicated in our sample sheet.
:::

You don't have to check this by eye, though:
the **Sample Status** section at the top of the report has a table that compares
the strandedness you specified in the sample sheet
with the strandedness that the pipeline inferred from the alignments,
and flags any samples for which these don't match.

Finally, the section **nf-core/rnaseq Software Versions** way at the bottom
lists the versions of all programs used by the pipeline!

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
#### Two more plots from the MultiQC report _(Click to expand)_

The **Qualimap** > **Gene Coverage Profile** plot shows average read-depth across
the length of genes/transcripts (averaged across all genes),
which helps to assess the amount of RNA degradation.
For poly-A selected libraries, RNA molecules "begin" at the 3' end
(right-hand side of the graph), so the more degradation there is,
the more you expect a higher read-depth towards the 3' end relative to that at the 5' end.

![](/img/multiqc_gene-coverage.png){fig-align="center" width="85%" .no-border fig-alt="MultiQC line plot of read coverage along gene bodies, with one line per sample. Coverage rises from about 100-200 at the 5' end to a plateau of about 400-500 around 30-70% of the transcript, then drops sharply at the very 3' end. Coverage at ~20% is lower than at ~80%."}

::: legend2
Here, the read depth at ~20% (near the 5' end) is clearly lower than at ~80% (near the 3' end), indicating some RNA degradation. Note that the sharp decreases at the _very_ end on each side are expected and do not indicate RNA degradation.
:::

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

The **STAR_SALMON DESeq2 PCA** plot is from a Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
run on the final gene count table,
showing overall patterns of gene expression similarity among samples.

![](/img/multiqc_pca.png){fig-align="center" width="80%" .no-border fig-alt="MultiQC PCA plot of samples (PC1 on the x-axis, PC2 on the y-axis). Samples form two distinct clusters: one with PC1 values around -35 to -18 and another, tighter one with PC1 values around 15 to 25."}

::: legend2
The samples form two distinct groups along PC1.
:::

:::

## Recap

In this lecture and [part I](w11b_nfcore1.qmd),
you have learned how to run an nf-core pipeline at OSC:

- Do a test run first, with `-profile test`, to check your setup
- Prepare the inputs: a sample sheet with your FASTQ files, and reference genome files
- Use a `nextflow.config` file to make Nextflow submit Slurm batch jobs
- Submit the main Nextflow process as a batch job itself, via a shell script
- Use a scratch dir as the work dir, and keep it until you're done with the run
- Rerun with `-resume` after failures or changes, so that only affected steps are rerun
- Find the key outputs: the MultiQC report and the gene count table

<br>
